lessons.title: Understanding Biosecurity on African Broiler Farms
lessons.body: Biosecurity is the set of practices that keep disease agents away from your birds and stop them from spreading if they do get in. For a broiler business in Africa, biosecurity is not a cost centre. It is an insurance policy that protects your feed conversion, your mortality curve, your market weight and your reputation. A single outbreak of Newcastle disease or highly pathogenic avian influenza can wipe out an entire flock in days and force you to cull, disinfect and start again with no income for six to eight weeks. That is a business failure, not just a veterinary problem. This lesson explains the three layers of biosecurity: structural, operational and procedural. Structural biosecurity is what you build. It includes the fence around the farm, the gate with a footbath, the concrete apron at the house entrance, the wire mesh over air inlets, the store room for feed, the changing room for staff and the isolation pen for sick birds. In many African settings, farms are built incrementally, so structural gaps are common. A farmer may start with one open-sided house and later add a second. The risk is that the second house shares equipment, boots and crates with the first. Even simple structures make a difference: a lockable gate, a roof that does not leak into the litter, a solid wall between the brooder and the feed store. Operational biosecurity is what you do every day. It includes limiting visitors, recording every person and vehicle that enters, using dedicated boots and overalls per house, washing hands before and after handling birds, and never borrowing crates, feeders or vaccines from another farm without disinfection. In Africa, many outbreaks trace back to shared transport. A trader collects birds from three farms in one pickup, then returns crates that have not been cleaned. The next farm loads birds into those crates and the cycle continues. Operational biosecurity also covers feed and water. Buy feed only from suppliers who seal bags and store them off the ground. Do not allow feed to sit in open bowls where wild birds can peck. Water tanks should be covered and chlorinated where possible. Rodents and wild birds are the most common mechanical vectors on small and medium farms. Procedural biosecurity is the written routine. It is the checklist that says: footbath refreshed daily, dead birds removed twice daily, litter turned or top-dressed, visitors logged, vaccines stored at the right temperature, and a quarantine period of at least 14 days for any new bird. Procedures must be simple enough that a farm worker can follow them without a supervisor. Use pictures if literacy is a challenge. Use local language for key steps. The goal is consistency, not paperwork. A farm that follows five simple rules every day is safer than one with a thick manual that nobody reads. Practical Africa-focused risks include: multi-age farms where chicks and older birds share air space; live bird markets that mix species and regions; free-range scavenging chickens near broiler houses; and seasonal winds that carry dust and feathers between farms. Each of these raises the challenge, but none makes biosecurity impossible. A small farm can use a simple three-zone layout: clean zone (feed store, office, chick area), transition zone (footbath, changing area), and dirty zone (loading ramp, dead bird pit, vehicle parking). Movement is always from clean to dirty, never back. Training workers is the highest-return investment. A worker who understands why he must not step from the dead bird pit into the brooder house will protect the flock better than any expensive disinfectant. Pay attention to incentives: if a worker is paid by the number of birds loaded, he may rush and skip disinfection. Build biosecurity into the job description and reward compliance. Record keeping matters for business. If you cannot show a buyer or a bank that you follow biosecurity, you cannot access premium markets, export or insurance. Simple records of visitor logs, mortality, feed intake and disinfection dates also help you spot problems early. A sudden rise in water consumption or a drop in feed intake is often the first sign of disease, before any bird looks sick. In summary, biosecurity on an African broiler farm is a daily habit built on three layers: structures that separate clean from dirty, operations that control people and equipment, and procedures that everyone follows. It costs little compared to the loss of a flock. Treat it as part of production, not as an extra. The next lesson will cover the specific disease threats you are protecting against and how to recognise them early.

lessons.title: Common Broiler Diseases in Africa and Early Warning Signs
lessons.body: Broiler production in Africa faces a predictable set of diseases. Knowing them helps you act fast, because in broilers the margin between a mild challenge and a catastrophic loss can be as short as 48 hours. This lesson covers the most important viral, bacterial, fungal and parasitic threats, their early signs, and the practical steps a farm manager can take before the vet arrives. Viral diseases are the most feared because they spread quickly and have no direct cure. Newcastle disease is endemic in many African countries. It affects the respiratory, nervous and digestive systems. Early signs in broilers include gasping, coughing, sneezing, watery eyes, greenish watery droppings, and a sudden drop in feed and water intake. Later you may see twisted necks, paralysis and high mortality. There is no treatment. Vaccination is the main defence, but vaccine handling is critical. A cold chain break of even a few hours can make the vaccine useless. Use a vaccine carrier with ice packs, reconstitute only enough for immediate use, and never mix vaccine with chlorinated water. Infectious bursal disease, also called Gumboro, attacks the immune system. Young birds between two and six weeks are most at risk. Signs include whitish watery droppings, vent pecking, depression, ruffled feathers and a sudden spike in deaths. Surviving birds are immunosuppressed and may die later from secondary infections. Strict cleaning between flocks and correct vaccination timing are essential. Avian influenza, especially highly pathogenic H5 and H7 strains, is a transboundary threat. Signs include sudden high mortality, swelling of the head and face, purple discolouration of the comb and wattles, and respiratory distress. Because it can infect humans, any suspicion must be reported immediately to veterinary authorities. Do not sell or move birds. Do not eat or sell eggs from a suspect flock. Biosecurity and rapid reporting are the only tools. Bacterial diseases are often secondary but can become primary under poor hygiene. Colibacillosis, caused by E. coli, is common where water lines are dirty or litter is wet. Signs include lethargy, poor growth, swollen joints and increased mortality. Improve water sanitation, reduce stocking density and use antibiotics only under veterinary direction with correct withdrawal periods. Fowl typhoid and pullorum disease, caused by Salmonella species, can cause white diarrhoea in chicks, pasty vents and high early mortality. Source chicks from a reputable hatchery and keep the brooder clean and dry. Mycoplasma infections cause chronic respiratory disease with snicking, coughing and swollen sinuses. They spread slowly but reduce feed conversion and cause condemnations at processing. Fungal and environmental problems are often overlooked. Aspergillosis comes from mouldy litter or feed. Signs include gasping without noise, rapid breathing and small yellow nodules in the lungs at post-mortem. Prevent it by keeping litter dry, storing feed off the floor and avoiding damp, poorly ventilated houses. Ammonia burn from wet litter damages the eyes and respiratory tract and opens the door to bacteria. Parasitic and protozoal diseases matter more in free-range and semi-intensive systems. Coccidiosis causes bloody droppings, huddling, pale combs and poor growth. It is controlled by clean litter, coccidiostats in feed and, where available, vaccination. External parasites such as mites and lice cause irritation, anaemia and reduced feed intake. Inspect birds weekly, especially under the wings and around the vent. Early warning signs are the same across most diseases: a change in behaviour, a change in feed or water intake, a change in droppings, and a change in mortality pattern. Train your workers to report these four changes immediately. A simple daily record sheet with columns for feed, water, deaths and observations is enough. Do not wait until birds are dying in large numbers. By then the disease has already spread through the house. Practical Africa-focused actions include: buy chicks only from hatcheries with a health certificate; keep a closed flock where possible; avoid mixing age groups; control rodents and wild birds; disinfect boots and equipment; and maintain a cold chain for vaccines. Work with a local vet or extension officer to set a vaccination programme for your area, because disease pressure varies by region and season. In the dry season, dust and wind spread respiratory agents. In the rainy season, wet litter increases coccidiosis and bacterial challenges. Know your local pattern. Finally, remember that disease diagnosis by phone is risky. If mortality exceeds one percent per day, or if you see nervous signs or bloody droppings, call a vet and submit samples. A post-mortem on a few fresh dead birds can save the rest of the flock. The cost of a diagnosis is small compared to the cost of guessing. The next lesson covers outbreak response: what to do in the first 24 hours.

lessons.title: Outbreak Response: The First 24 Hours
lessons.body: When disease strikes a broiler flock, the first 24 hours determine whether you lose a few birds or the whole business. This lesson gives a step-by-step response plan that works on small, medium and large farms in Africa. The plan assumes you have already noticed one of the early warning signs from the previous lesson: a drop in feed or water intake, a change in droppings, a rise in mortality, or unusual behaviour. Step one: stop all movement. Do not sell, move or give away any bird, crate, feed bag or equipment. Do not allow visitors, traders or other farmers onto the farm. Put a lock on the gate. If you have multiple houses, restrict staff to one house each and do not let them move between houses. If you must move between houses, change boots and overalls and wash hands. Movement is how disease spreads from one house to the next and from your farm to your neighbour. Step two: isolate the affected house. Mark it clearly. Use dedicated boots, overalls, buckets and tools for that house only. Do not share feeders, drinkers or crates with other houses. If the affected house is close to a healthy house, increase ventilation in the healthy house and reduce dust movement. If possible, use a temporary solid barrier such as a plastic sheet or tarpaulin between houses. Step three: call for help. Contact your veterinarian, extension officer or a trusted poultry health professional immediately. Describe the signs, the age of the birds, the mortality rate and the vaccination history. If you suspect avian influenza or Newcastle disease, report to the veterinary authorities. Do not wait for a confirmation to act. Early reporting can trigger official support, laboratory testing and compensation programmes in some countries. Step four: collect information. Write down the date and time you first noticed a problem. Count dead birds and remove them in sealed bags or a covered pit. Record feed and water intake for the last three days. Check the vaccination records, feed delivery dates and any recent visitors. This information helps the vet make a diagnosis and helps you prevent the next outbreak. Step five: submit samples correctly. If the vet asks for samples, use clean, sterile containers. For live birds, submit a few sick birds that have not been treated. For dead birds, submit fresh carcasses, not decomposed ones. Keep samples cool, not frozen, and deliver them quickly. In many African settings, the nearest laboratory may be hours away, so plan the transport before you collect. Step six: treat only under veterinary direction. Do not pour antibiotics into drinking water without a diagnosis. Wrong treatment wastes money, creates resistance and may leave residues in meat. If the vet prescribes treatment, follow the dose, the duration and the withdrawal period exactly. Withdrawal periods matter for market access. Selling meat with antibiotic residues can destroy your reputation and break the law. Step seven: increase biosecurity immediately. Refresh footbaths. Use a disinfectant that works against the suspected agent. Most viruses are killed by common disinfectants, but organic matter such as manure and litter reduces effectiveness. Clean first, then disinfect. Increase rodent control. Cover feed. Keep wild birds out. If the outbreak is in one house, do everything possible to protect the others. Step eight: plan for the worst. If mortality is high and the disease is confirmed as highly pathogenic avian influenza or a similar serious threat, you may be required to cull the flock. Culling is painful financially and emotionally, but it stops the spread and may be the only way to protect other farms and your own future. Work with authorities on humane culling, disposal and compensation. Do not hide the problem. Hiding it usually makes it worse. Step nine: clean and disinfect after the flock is gone. Remove all litter, manure and feed. Wash the house with detergent, then disinfect. Pay attention to corners, cracks, fans, feeders and drinkers. Leave the house empty for at least two weeks, longer if possible. If you have multiple houses, clean them one at a time and do not move equipment from dirty to clean areas. Step ten: review and learn. After the outbreak, sit with your team and write down what happened. What was the likely source? Was it a visitor, a feed delivery, a new batch of chicks, a wild bird, or a break in vaccination? What worked in your response? What failed? Update your biosecurity plan. Train workers again. Restock only when the house is fully dry and disinfected, and only with chicks from a reputable hatchery. Practical Africa-focused notes: keep a phone list of your vet, extension officer and local veterinary authority. Keep a small emergency fund for diagnostics and disinfectants. If you share a truck or crates with other farms, clean and disinfect before and after every trip. If you buy from live bird markets, quarantine new birds away from the main flock. If you have neighbours with poultry, talk to them about biosecurity. Disease does not respect fences. A coordinated local response is stronger than any single farm. Finally, remember that an outbreak is not the end of your business if you respond fast and honestly. Many farms recover and become stronger because they learn what went wrong. The next lesson covers vaccination programmes and cold chain management.

lessons.title: Vaccination Programmes and Cold Chain Management
lessons.body: Vaccination is the backbone of disease prevention in broiler production, but in Africa the biggest challenge is not the vaccine itself. It is the cold chain, the timing and the technique. A vaccine that has been exposed to heat, sunlight or chlorine is money wasted and a false sense of security. This lesson explains how to build a practical vaccination programme for broilers and how to keep vaccines effective from the supplier to the bird. Start with the principle: broilers have a short life, usually five to seven weeks. There is little time to build immunity. Vaccines must be given at the right age, in the right way, and only when the birds are healthy. Sick birds should not be vaccinated. If a flock is already showing respiratory signs or diarrhoea, vaccinating can make things worse. Treat the immediate problem first, then vaccinate when the birds recover. A typical broiler vaccination programme in Africa may include the following. Day one: Marek's disease vaccine is usually given at the hatchery. If you hatch your own chicks, you must arrange this. Newcastle disease vaccine may be given at day one or day seven depending on the local strain and the vaccine type. Infectious bronchitis is often combined with Newcastle in a single vaccine. Day seven to ten: Newcastle disease booster, often with infectious bronchitis. Day fourteen to eighteen: Infectious bursal disease, also called Gumboro, if the local challenge is high. Some programmes use a second Gumboro dose at day twenty-one to twenty-four. Day twenty-one to twenty-eight: Newcastle disease booster if the flock is kept longer or if disease pressure is high. This is a guide, not a prescription. Your local vet or extension officer should adjust it for your area, your season and the vaccines available. Some countries have different strains and different vaccine schedules. Always follow the manufacturer's instructions and local regulations. Now the cold chain. Most poultry vaccines are live attenuated vaccines. They must be kept between two and eight degrees Celsius. Freezing can kill some vaccines, especially those for Newcastle and infectious bronchitis. Heat destroys them quickly. A vaccine left on a dashboard in the sun can lose potency in minutes. Invest in a good cooler box or vaccine carrier with ice packs. Do not use ordinary ice directly on the vaccine vials. Wrap the ice packs in paper or cloth to prevent freezing. Keep a thermometer in the cooler and check it before you leave the store and when you arrive at the farm. If you do not have a refrigerator, buy ice or use a kerosene or solar fridge. Solar direct-drive refrigerators are increasingly available in Africa and are a good option for farms without reliable electricity. When you receive vaccines, check the expiry date, the label and the temperature. If the ice packs are melted or the vial is warm, do not use it. Record the batch number and the date received. Store vaccines in the middle of the fridge, not on the door and not against the freezer compartment. The door is the warmest part and the freezer can freeze the vaccine. Reconstitute vaccine only with the diluent supplied by the manufacturer. Never use chlorinated water, because chlorine kills live vaccine viruses. If you must use tap water, let it stand overnight or use distilled water. Reconstitute only enough for immediate use. Do not save reconstituted vaccine for the next day. Use it within one to two hours, and keep it cool while you work. Vaccination technique matters as much as the vaccine. For eye drops, put one drop in the eye and wait until the bird blinks. For nostril drops, put one drop in one nostril and hold the beak closed briefly. For drinking water, remove all water and let the birds thirst for one to two hours before giving the vaccine. Use enough drinkers so that every bird can drink at the same time. Add skimmed milk powder to the water to protect the vaccine virus, but do not use chlorine or disinfectants. For injections, use a clean needle and change it regularly. Do not inject more than the recommended dose. Handle birds gently to avoid stress and injury. Record every vaccination: date, age, vaccine name, batch number, method, dose and the person who did it. This record helps you trace problems and proves to buyers and regulators that you follow good practice. If you sell to supermarkets, hotels or exporters, they may ask for vaccination records. Keep them for at least one year. Practical Africa-focused tips: buy vaccines only from reputable suppliers with a cold chain. Avoid buying from open markets where vaccines may have been stored badly. If you share a vaccine carrier with other farms, clean and disinfect it between uses. Plan your vaccination days around the weather. Do not vaccinate during the hottest part of the day. Early morning or late afternoon is better. If you use a vaccination team, make sure they are trained and that they do not move from a sick farm to a healthy one without changing clothes and boots. Finally, remember that vaccination is not a substitute for biosecurity. A vaccinated flock can still get sick if the challenge is high or if the vaccine was not handled correctly. Use vaccination together with clean water, dry litter, good ventilation and limited visitors. The next lesson covers cleaning, disinfection and farm records.

lessons.title: Cleaning, Disinfection and Record Keeping for Broiler Farms
lessons.body: Cleaning and disinfection between flocks is one of the most cost-effective biosecurity practices on a broiler farm. It breaks the disease cycle and gives the next batch of chicks a clean start. Record keeping turns those practices into a business asset. This lesson covers the practical steps for cleaning and disinfection in African conditions and the records that every broiler farm should keep. Start with the principle: cleaning removes organic matter, and disinfection kills the remaining germs. If you disinfect a dirty surface, the disinfectant is neutralised by manure, litter and grease. So the order is always dry clean, wash, rinse, disinfect, dry. Step one: remove all birds and all movable equipment. Feeders, drinkers, crates, fans and tools should be taken out and cleaned separately. Step two: dry clean. Remove all litter, manure, feed and dust. Scrape the floor, walls and ceiling. Pay attention to corners, cracks, vents and the area around feeders and drinkers. Bag the litter and manure and move it far from the house. If you use it as fertiliser, compost it properly to kill pathogens. Step three: wash. Use a detergent or soap and warm water if available. A pressure washer is ideal, but a brush and bucket work if you are thorough. Wash from the top down: ceiling, walls, equipment, floor. Step four: rinse. Remove all soap and dirt. Do not let dirty water pool in the house. Step five: disinfect. Choose a disinfectant that is effective against the diseases you are worried about. Common choices include glutaraldehyde, quaternary ammonium compounds, bleach and hydrogen peroxide. Follow the label for dilution and contact time. Contact time is critical. Many farmers spray and immediately rinse, which does not give the disinfectant time to work. Leave it on the surface for the recommended time, usually ten to thirty minutes. Step six: dry. Let the house dry completely before bringing in new litter or chicks. Moisture encourages bacteria and fungi. Step seven: replace litter and equipment. Use clean, dry litter such as wood shavings, rice husks or chopped straw. Do not use mouldy or damp material. Set up the brooder and drinkers. Step eight: fumigate if possible. Some farms use formaldehyde fumigation, but it is dangerous and should only be done by trained people with proper protective equipment. In many African settings, thorough cleaning and disinfection is enough. Step nine: keep the house empty for at least seven to fourteen days. This downtime helps break the disease cycle. If you have multiple houses, clean them one at a time and do not move dirty equipment into clean areas. Practical Africa-focused challenges include limited water, unreliable electricity, expensive disinfectants and shared equipment. You can manage these by planning ahead. Store water in tanks. Use a solar pump if possible. Buy disinfectant in bulk with other farmers to reduce cost. Label equipment by house and do not share it. If you must share crates or trucks, clean and disinfect them before and after every use. Now record keeping. Records are not paperwork for its own sake. They help you spot problems, prove your practices to buyers and lenders, and make better decisions. Keep these records for every flock: date of placement, number of chicks, breed, hatchery and batch number; daily mortality; daily feed and water intake; vaccination dates, vaccine names, batch numbers and methods; any medication, dose, duration and withdrawal period; cleaning and disinfection dates and products used; visitor log with names, dates and purpose; and final results: total feed used, total weight sold, feed conversion ratio, mortality percentage and income. A simple notebook or a wall chart works. If you have a smartphone, use a simple spreadsheet or a free farm record app. The key is consistency. Record every day, even when nothing seems wrong. A sudden change in feed or water intake is often the first sign of disease. If you have records, you can see the change and act early. Records also help you calculate your cost of production. Many broiler farmers do not know their true cost per kilogram. Without records, you cannot tell whether you are making a profit or a loss. With records, you can compare flocks, identify your best and worst batches, and negotiate better prices with buyers. For market access, buyers increasingly ask for evidence of biosecurity and vaccination. A simple record book can open doors to supermarkets, hotels, restaurants and export markets. It also helps with insurance and credit. Banks and insurers are more likely to support a farm that can show consistent records. Finally, review your records at the end of every flock. Ask: what went well? What went wrong? What will I change next time? Share the lessons with your workers. A farm that learns from its records improves with every batch. In summary, cleaning and disinfection protect your next flock, and records protect your business. Together they turn biosecurity from a cost into a competitive advantage. Use the steps in this lesson to build a routine that works for your farm, your climate and your budget. Then repeat it every flock, without shortcuts.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Vaccine Handling, Cold Chain and On-Farm Vaccination Technique for African Broiler Farms

On a broiler farm, a vaccine that has been overheated, frozen, or mixed incorrectly is not a vaccine at all â it is a wasted input, a false sense of security, and a direct hit to your gross margin. In African production systems, where a single Newcastle disease outbreak can wipe out 60â100% of a flock within days, the difference between a profitable cycle and a total loss often comes down to how the vaccine vial was handled between the hatchery and the drinker line. This lesson gives you the practical reference you need to protect that investment: temperature thresholds, dilution tables, technique standards, and record-keeping discipline that stand up to buyer audits and lender scrutiny.

Treat vaccination as a business process, not a chore. Every dose costs money; every failed dose costs money twice â once when you buy it, and again when disease breaks through. The figures below let you calculate what poor handling actually costs your operation.

Why This Matters to Your Bottom Line

Vaccine failure is rarely dramatic. It looks like a flock that "just doesn't perform": higher mortality in week 3, uneven growth, increased feed conversion ratio, and a processor or buyer who discounts your birds. When you trace it back, the cause is often a broken cold chain, a chlorine-contaminated water line, or a vaccinator who moved too fast. The tables below give you the numbers to plan against.

Sources: Aviagen Broiler Management Handbook (2022); University of Georgia Cooperative Extension, Vaccination of Commercial Broilers; ILRI smallholder poultry health notes. Volumes assume moderate ambient temperature (22â28 Â°C); increase by 20â30% in hot, dry conditions above 30 Â°C.

â  SAFETY WARNING â VACCINES, CHEMICALS AND WATER QUALITY

  • Never freeze live vaccines. Freezing breaks the vial seal and destroys the vaccine. Discard any vial that has been frozen â do not use it "just in case".
  • Never use expired or heat-damaged vaccine. If the vial was warm to the touch or left in the sun, discard it. A failed vaccine is worse than no vaccine because it creates false confidence.
  • Chlorine and disinfectants kill live vaccines. Flush drinker lines with clean water 24 hours before water vaccination. Do not add chlorine, iodine, or acidifiers to vaccine water.
  • Protect yourself. When handling reconstituted vials, avoid needle-stick injuries during injection routes (e.g. inactivated vaccines). Dispose of needles and vials in a sharps container â never in the feed store or open pit.
  • Store vaccines away from food, feed and children. Use a dedicated vaccine fridge with a locked door and a thermometer. Never store vaccines in a domestic fridge alongside food.
  • Report adverse reactions. If birds show swelling, mortality or unusual signs within 24 hours of vaccination, contact your veterinarian and the vaccine supplier immediately.

Calculating the Cost of a Broken Cold Chain

Take a 5,000-bird broiler cycle. A Newcastle disease vaccination programme costs roughly USD 0.015â0.03 per bird in most African markets â about USD 75â150 per cycle. If cold chain failure means the vaccine fails and Newcastle breaks through at 30% mortality, you lose 1,500 birds. At a farm-gate value of USD 3.00 per bird, that is USD 4,500 lost, plus feed consumed by birds that never reach market. The vaccine cost was 2â3% of the loss. That ratio is why cold chain discipline is a business decision, not a technical detail.

Use this same calculation with your own numbers before you decide to "save money" on a cheaper cooler box or skip a thermometer. The economics are not close.

Quick Reference Checklist â Before, During and After Vaccination

  • Before: Confirm vaccine name, batch number, expiry date and storage history. Check the vial seal is intact and the freeze-dry cake is not melted or discoloured.
  • Before: Calibrate your thermometer. Record fridge temperature twice daily â morning and evening â in a log book.
  • Before: Withhold water for 1.5â2 hours (never more than 2.5 hours in hot weather). Flush drinker lines with clean, non-chlorinated water.
  • During: Reconstitute only the number of vials you can use within 2 hours. Keep the remaining vials in the cold box, not on the farm table.
  • During: Add skimmed milk powder (2â2.5 g per litre) to neutralise residual chlorine. Stir gently â do not shake or create foam.
  • During: Walk the house slowly. Ensure every bird has access to a drinker. Check that water lines are at the correct height and pressure.
  • After: Record vaccine name, batch, expiry, time of reconstitution, time of completion, number of birds vaccinated, and any reactions observed.
  • After: Burn or disinfect empty vials and packaging. Never reuse vials. Wash hands and change clothes before entering another house.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Good Practices for the Meat Industry (biosecurity and poultry health sections)
  • WOAH (OIE) â Terrestrial Animal Health Code: poultry vaccination and disease control
  • Aviagen â Broiler Management Handbook (vaccination, water quality, biosecurity)
  • University of Georgia Cooperative Extension â Vaccination of Commercial Broilers
  • ILRI â Animal Health and Poultry Vaccine Delivery in Africa

Vaccination is one of the highest-return inputs on a broiler farm â but only when the cold chain holds, the water is clean, and the technique is right. Build the checklist into your standard operating procedure, train every worker who touches a vaccine vial, and keep records that a buyer or lender can trust. In African broiler production, the farms that survive disease pressure are the ones that treat vaccine handling as seriously as they treat feed and cash flow.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of the brooding period in broiler production?
options: A) To provide warmth and care for young chicks
B) To increase feed conversion ratio
quiz.explanation: Brooding provides heat, water, feed, and protection to chicks during their first days of life.

quiz.q: Which environmental factor is most critical to monitor during brooding?
quiz.explanation: Temperature control is essential because chicks cannot regulate body temperature well in early life.

quiz.q: What does feed conversion ratio FCR measure in broiler production?
options: C) Feed consumed per unit of body weight gain
quiz.explanation: FCR is the amount of feed required to produce one unit of live weight gain.

quiz.q: Which ventilation strategy helps remove excess moisture and ammonia from a broiler house?
quiz.explanation: Minimum ventilation exchanges stale air while maintaining adequate house temperature.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of heat stress in broiler chickens?
quiz.explanation: Panting and wing spreading are behavioral responses used by birds to lose heat.

quiz.q: Why is biosecurity important in broiler production?
options: B) To prevent disease introduction and spread
quiz.explanation: Biosecurity measures limit pathogens and protect flock health and productivity.

quiz.q: What is the recommended action when broiler litter becomes wet and caked?
options: C) Remove or replace wet litter
quiz.explanation: Wet litter can cause ammonia buildup, footpad lesions, and respiratory problems.

quiz.q: Which parameter is commonly used to determine when broilers are ready for market?
options: D) Target live weight and age
quiz.explanation: Broilers are typically marketed when they reach the desired live weight at a planned age.
